newsitem.title: PERU: Peru mother begs for rebel corpse, remembers past.
newsitem.headline: Peru mother begs for rebel corpse, remembers past.

text.p: Like other Peruvians, Luz Villoslada's mother occasionally saw her daughter's face on television in the window of the besieged Japanese ambassador's house during the 18-week hostage siege.

Now all the mother has left of her guerrilla daughter is a corpse -- and maybe not even that, as the Lima morgue refused to hand over the body of the 16-year-old girl who liked Mexican soap operas and once wanted to be a nurse.

Her mother, Eligia Rodriguez, fears the military secretly buried her, as it reportedly did the other Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) militants killed in the Peruvian military's raid on the Japanese mansion.
Villoslada and the 13 other MRTA guerrillas who held 72 hostages in the residence were all slain in the gunbattle, in which elite troops rescued 71 of the 72 hostages.
"We recognised her when we saw her on television in January, wearing one of those terrorist scarfs (over her face). We recorded the image" on the VCR, she said.

The particular poignancy of Villoslada's case was that her mother had not seen her since 1993, when, her mother said, the girl was virtually kidnapped by acquaitances active in the MRTA near their home in the Amazon jungle.
"The morocos (armed men in uniforms) took away Luz, dragged her away by her feet and hands," Luz's sister told their mother after accompanying her sibling to fetch water from a well in May 1993.

In Lima on Friday, the mother cried and remembered the moment when she found out that her daughter had been kidnapped. She remembered running barefoot to the place where Luz had last been seen to try to get her back.
Now she is trying to reclaim her dead daughter's body.
"I only want her body. I want to see her close-up even if she is dead. It's been four years since she was last by my side. Now I'm told she's buried as an unknown," Rodriguez said.

Villoslada and 13 other MRTA guerrillas burst from obscurity into the international spotlight last Dec. 17 when they stormed the residence of Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki during a cocktail party and took hundreds of hostages. They later released all but 72 of the hostages.

Rodriguez said she never knew her daughter had friends in MRTA. "We didn't know anything about the rebels until they took her away," she said. "She never mentioned that she had friends or that she sympathised with the terrorists. She never talked about them," Luz's brother Luciano said.
Her mother added: "She was a normal girl, a very good (person) and hard worker. Saturdays and Sundays she sold pastries which I made."
